Bounded idea units:
U-S-0161-C04-SR-01 (212-214): An evaluation task could be to track "dead topics": identifying ideas that were explored in the project's history but were later abandoned. This is difficult because it requires finding the initial mention and then confirming its absence or an explicit decision to drop it in later meetings.
U-S-0161-C04-SR-02 (215-216): A simple retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach is insufficient for tracking abandoned topics because it would find all related mentions across meetings, but it cannot understand the temporal sequence or identify a final decision to discontinue an idea.
U-S-0161-C04-SR-03 (217-218): An alternative evaluation method, inspired by a Springer paper, is to verify if the system correctly identifies the final, jointly-agreed-upon decisions, distinguishing them from the scattered, preliminary discussions that led to them.
U-S-0161-C04-SR-04 (220-223): Another evaluation approach for non-linear meetings involves checking if the system's summary covers all points from a predefined agenda. This method requires an expert-generated ground truth and is relevant for defining the structure of long-term summarization.
U-S-0161-C04-SR-05 (224-225): As a next step, the team should redefine their memory architecture and review the "Digital Me" paper to understand its methods for determining relevancy.
U-S-0161-C04-SR-06 (226-227): The "Digital Me" paper's evaluation method tests the factual correctness of the model's outputs regarding recent plans, self-introduction, and high-level opinions, likely using RAG over a person's entire history.
U-S-0161-C04-SR-07 (228-230): A proposed method for evaluation is to use synthetic data. The team could create a fake history with a "planted" topic that is introduced and then abandoned, then test if the system correctly excludes this topic from a list of current to-dos, thereby reflecting the latest decision.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-01 (231-234): An experiment involving approximately 40 API calls (described as running 'Ethereum' 13 times with ~3 runs each) cost about 75 units (rising from 14 to 91). This usage was identified as 37 API calls made the previous day.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-02 (236-236): A potential issue was raised regarding Google Cloud account region restrictions, based on a past experience where a US-based account faced problems in Taiwan. A suggestion was made to test the lab's account to see if similar issues occur.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-03 (237-238): The Google Cloud free trial provides $300 USD in credits after binding a credit card. It was noted that this could be misleading for Taiwanese users, as the UI is in Chinese but the amount is in USD, not TWD.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-04 (239-240): There is a separate free credit of 9000 units (presumably TWD) that expires after a set period. There was uncertainty whether the period is 30 days or three months. This credit is used before the credit card is charged and resets to zero upon expiration.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-05 (241-241): A question was raised whether the Google Cloud free credits apply to the Gemini API, or if Gemini API usage is billed separately from the general Google Cloud platform.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-06 (242-247): It was clarified that AI Studio is not billed separately; its usage is integrated with and billed through a linked Google Cloud Project. The Google Cloud Project is the central entity for managing billing, and an API key from AI Studio is tied to a specific project's billing account.
U-S-0231-C01-SR-07 (248-250): The team decided on a strategy to maximize free credits: they will first exhaust the current account's remaining 9000-unit free credit, which expires soon (around April 26th). Only after that will they activate a new free trial on another account to start a fresh 3-month credit period.
